content:
Plan your service around the people the venue can safely accommodate. Include how they arrive, move through the building and leave, rather than considering only the people in their seats.

Start with the approved occupancy and your actual room layout. Then use attendance estimates and on-site observations to plan admissions and respond to crowding.

---

## Confirm the limit with the local authority

In the United States, building codes mostly belong to state and local governments. NIST explains that jurisdictions adopt model codes and may change their provisions. Begin with your local fire marshal and building department when confirming the occupancy limit for your proposed worship use.

Ask the owner for the occupancy documentation and ask the local authority which rooms and arrangements it covers. In Fairfax County, Virginia, for example, an application for a maximum occupant load posting requires floor plans, seating diagrams and other documents about occupancy limits. Its guidance explicitly includes places of worship.

<Callout type="important">
The agency guidance here was checked October 16, 2026. Confirm current occupancy requirements and the approved layout with your local fire marshal and building department. The Fairfax examples describe that locality's process.
</Callout>

---

## Check the setup you will actually use

A different room arrangement can need a different occupancy assessment. Fairfax notes that spaces with multiple configurations may have different seating diagrams and occupant loads. Ask about your proposed setup before changing it.

Bring a drawing that shows the seating, stage, tables and equipment alongside exits and aisles. Fairfax's submission guidance asks for these details, including exit-door and aisle widths. Ask which approved drawing your setup team should follow.

Walk the routes before admitting people. Check that designated exits are available for immediate use, paths are unobstructed and exit signs remain visible. Fairfax's assembly checklist asks operators to check these conditions.

<Callout type="warning">
Keep crowds out of exit aisles and doorways. Fairfax's checklist addresses obstructions caused by people as well as objects. An empty chair does not excuse a blocked exit route.
</Callout>

---

## Include people beyond the worship seats

Count the people using the space, including those serving. Fairfax's self-inspection checklist asks whether the number of persons inside the occupancy is limited to the approved occupant load. It does not ask only about seated guests.

Ask the local authority how the building's limits apply to the worship room, children's rooms and shared areas. Ask how children, volunteers and people moving between rooms should be included in the count for your arrangement.

For practical planning, the UK's Health and Safety Executive, or HSE, advises considering young people and people with disabilities when assessing crowd risks. Use its event guidance here as planning advice, with local officials confirming the applicable US requirements.

---

## Forecast attendance before setting the plan

HSE suggests considering past attendance, pre-event registration, publicity and particularly busy days when estimating turnout. Use those inputs for your service rather than assuming every service will draw the same crowd.

| Planning input | Question to answer |
|---|---|
| Previous attendance | What happened at comparable services or events? |
| Registration | What interest have people already expressed? |
| Publicity | How widely is this service being promoted? |
| Special activities | Might these bring additional visitors? |
| Weather and transport | Could these affect attendance? |

Consider how visitors will find their way. HSE notes that guests may be unfamiliar with a venue's layout. Include entrances, seating areas and exits in the information your team provides.

---

## Keep a live count during the service

HSE recommends monitoring both the total number of people and their distribution. Watch entrances, exits, queues and confined areas. A total below the venue limit does not tell you whether a particular doorway is becoming crowded.

Hand counters at entry and exit points are among HSE's suggested counting methods. Choose a method your team can maintain while people arrive and depart. Keep the current count available to the person coordinating admissions.

Give counters time to do the job. HSE advises checking that staff who monitor crowds alongside other duties have enough opportunity to monitor, or considering additional help during busy periods.

<Callout type="tip">
Watch the queues as well as the count. HSE recommends monitoring how people are distributed, not only the overall total. Ask someone to report developing congestion while others track admissions.
</Callout>

---

## Plan the handover between services

HSE identifies arrival, movement inside the venue and departure as separate crowd-management concerns. For larger crowds, it suggests phased arrivals and departures, including staggered event times.

If you are considering another service, plan what happens while one congregation leaves and the next arrives. Review entrances, waiting areas and departure routes with the venue. Check where opposing flows of people could meet.

Do not let waiting lines block emergency access routes. HSE advises providing a safe way out of a queue without forcing people against the queue or into moving vehicles. Include parking directions in the arrival information where people will drive.

---

## Decide how to respond before capacity is reached

Where arrivals might exceed safe capacity, HSE advises planning how to monitor numbers and redirect excess people. It also identifies overflow space as an option to consider. Discuss that option with the owner and local fire marshal before offering it.

Ask which proposed overflow room is approved for the intended use and what limit applies there. Keep the response within the confirmed occupancy arrangements. Train the team to follow that plan rather than allowing more people into a full space.

Give guests clear directions before and during the service. HSE recommends using visitor information, signs and stewards to direct people toward safe routes and away from prohibited areas.

---

## Brief the team and review what happened

HSE advises giving volunteers the information and training needed for their work, with supervision suited to the event's risks. Before opening, confirm these arrangements:

- [ ] Volunteers know their crowd-management duties.
- [ ] The team knows how to report crowding.
- [ ] A coordinator can receive reports and direct a response.
- [ ] Emergency arrangements are ready.

After the service, discuss problems and successes and revise the plan where needed. HSE recommends debriefing after events, particularly after significant incidents or when considering changes to layouts or procedures.

<Callout type="scripture">
*"But all things must be done properly and in an orderly manner."* — 1 Corinthians 14:40 (LSB)
</Callout>
excerpt: Confirm local occupancy limits, check your service layout, count people and plan queues, turnover and overflow before the room fills.
title: Planning Services Around Room Capacity
